name: Brunello di Montalcino

known.via: English Wikipedia "Brunello di Montalcino" (a wine place on Wikidata)

climate: Seasons this warm ripen Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sangiovese, Sémillon and Cabernet Franc fully without cooking off their freshness.
Sangiovese, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon sit in their sweet spot, so the wines can show the style they are known for.
Rain picks up at harvest. Growers race to pick before rot sets in, and vintages vary more.

soil.rock: Limestone makes alkaline soil that drains well yet can hold water for the vines. It is usually planted to grapes valued for their acidity.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its high pH can starve vines of iron and yellow the leaves, so growers plant lime-tolerant rootstocks.

land: The high ground runs about 4°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.

winkler: Good for generous crops of standard to good wine.

sheet.place: Brunello is 100% Sangiovese from the hills around Montalcino, south of Siena. It ages at least two years in oak and goes on sale five years after the harvest year, six for Riserva.

claims.claim: Brunello di Montalcino is made from Sangiovese only. The vineyards must be planted only to Sangiovese.

The DOCG zone is the whole administrative territory of the comune of Montalcino, province of Siena, as it stood on 30 November 2011. It is one commune and has no separate villages or zones in the rules.

Montalcino is in south-east Tuscany, about 40 km south of Siena. The territory covers 243.62 square km, roughly square, with sides of about 15 km. It is bounded by the valleys of the Orcia, Asso and Ombrone rivers.
The hill is about 40 km in a straight line from the sea to the west and about 100 km from the Apennine chain to the east.

The territory runs from about 120 m above sea level along the rivers to about 650 m near Poggio Civitella, its highest point. The rules set no minimum or maximum vineyard altitude. They only ask for ground that ripens grapes well.

The disciplinare says the hill has many soil types because it formed in different geological eras. They trace to sandstones (sometimes mixed with limestone), alberese and galestro, and to mixed textures that lean sandy in some places and clayey in others.
The soils tend to be low in organic matter and calcareous, with little water in summer. This keeps Sangiovese vigour modest and yields low.
The lowest ground has relatively loose soils. Higher up, the soil is denser and holds stony particles from weathered marl and limestone.

The hill has many slopes with different exposures. This gives many small microclimates, even close together. In general, north-facing slopes ripen later and give racier wines. South- and west-facing slopes give more powerful ones.

North side (the area around Montalcino town and Montosoli, toward Buonconvento): cooler, on calcareous galestro marl. Wines are described as elegant and perfumed, with finer tannins and a salty, mineral edge. Northern sites tend to pick later than southern ones.
Montosoli, a hill just north of the town, is given as about 250 to 300 m, facing south-east, on galestro and marl.
North-east, around Torrenieri: compact clay soils and more tannic, robust wines.

South side in general: warmer and drier than the north. Lower ground has heavier clay and gives powerful, tannic wines. Higher, stonier ground drains better and gives finer wines. Wine Spectator calls the south richer and more opulent.

Castelnuovo dell'Abate (south-east, near Mount Amiata): called the warmest subzone, with south-facing slopes cooled by Amiata's night air. This gives a wide day-to-night swing that slows ripening and keeps acidity. Soils mix sand, clay and limestone, with galestro higher up. Vineyards are given at about 150 to 400 m.

Sant'Angelo in Colle (south-west): south-facing vineyards in the open sun, shaped by Mount Amiata's weather. Soils have more clay and sand. Altitude is given as about 300 to 400 m. The wines are known as the most muscular and powerful Brunellos, with deep colour and firm tannins.

Montalcino has no official subzones. The disciplinare names none. Writers use informal areas such as north, south, Castelnuovo dell'Abate, Sant'Angelo, Torrenieri, Camigliano, Tavernelle and Bosco. Kerin O'Keefe has proposed eight for labelling.

The climate is Mediterranean and tends to be dry, with some continental traits because the hill sits between the sea and the Apennines. Average rainfall is about 700 mm a year, mostly in spring and autumn. Snow is possible above 400 m in winter.

Mid-slope vineyards are not troubled by fog, frost or late frost. Frequent wind keeps the vines healthy. The growing season is mild with many clear days. Ripening is gradual and the late summer and early autumn are cooler, with large day to night swings.
Mount Amiata to the south (1,740 m) shelters the territory from storms and hail.
Wikipedia says Montalcino has the lowest rainfall of any Tuscan DOCG (about 700 mm versus about 900 mm in Chianti) and ripens up to a week earlier than nearby Montepulciano.

Brunello must age at least 24 months in oak containers of any size. The disciplinare sets no barrel size. Up to 6% of the wine in aging may be held in other containers. After that it needs at least 4 months in bottle (6 for Riserva).
Brunello cannot be sold before 1 January of the year after the end of five years, counted from the harvest year.

Brunello Riserva follows the same rule with six years, so release is one year later. Lots meant for Riserva must be separated in the cellar registers by 31 December of the fifth year. Riserva has no longer wood time than the base wine in the text, only the longer wait and 6 months in bottle.
Brunello that does not meet the rules can be declassified to Rosso di Montalcino DOC, keeping the Brunello yield per hectare.

Maximum yield is 8 t/ha (54.4 hl of wine), or 7 t/ha with a vigna or vigneto mention. Natural alcohol must reach 12.0% (12.5% with vigna). The maximum wine yield is 68% of the grapes. New plantings since 2016 need at least 4,000 vines per hectare.

At release the wine must be intense ruby tending to garnet. It must be dry, warm, a little tannic, robust, harmonious and persistent. It needs at least 12.5% alcohol, 5.0 g/l total acidity and 26.0 g/l extract.

The disciplinare describes the aroma as intense, persistent and ethereal, with undergrowth, aromatic wood, small fruits, light vanilla and jam. It says the wine keeps a minimum of ten and up to thirty years depending on the vintage.
The disciplinare recommends a wide glass and a serving temperature of about 18 to 20 C.

Everything from winemaking to bottling must happen inside the zone. Bottles must be dark Bordeaux-type glass with a one-piece cork. Agglomerated corks and other closures are banned. The vintage must be on the label.
Brunello di Montalcino was approved as a DOC by decree of 28 March 1966 (Gazzetta Ufficiale 30 June 1966) and as a DOCG by decree of 1 July 1980 (Gazzetta Ufficiale 15 November 1980).
Brunello di Montalcino was among the first wines to get the DOCG, in 1980.

The disciplinare names Clemente Santi as the forerunner of Brunello. His 1865 Vino Scelto (Brunello) won a silver medal in 1869. Brunello of Raffaello Padelletti and Riccardo Paccagnini won prizes in the 1890s and early 1900s. Production fell in the early 1900s. Few producers kept it going between the wars, and after World War II some agreed the production rules.

Wikipedia adds that Clemente Santi isolated Sangiovese plantings for a 100% varietal wine, and that his grandson Ferruccio Biondi-Santi released a long-aged first modern Brunello in 1888. It also notes a red called Brunello in the area in the early 14th century.

The origin of the name Montalcino is uncertain. One theory is Mons Lucinus, the mount of Lucina, a Roman goddess. The other is Mons Ilcinus, the mount of holm oaks (lecci). The three holm oaks on the town's coat of arms support the second.
Brunello is a local nickname, from the word for brown, for a vine once thought to be separate. A provincial commission in Siena found in 1879 that it was Sangiovese.
Rosso di Montalcino DOC was set up in 1984. It lets producers release a younger Sangiovese while Brunello ages.
